records.our_prose: Collards are leafy and N-hungry, and steady nitrogen drives the deep green color and tender growth that make the crop. Work a balanced fertilizer into the bed at planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks later, and feed again after a heavy cutting to push new leaves. Extension guides commonly cite a nitrogen side-dressing such as calcium nitrate or 27-3-3 along the row; on long-held plants a feed every 3 to 4 weeks keeps them productive. Avoid overdoing nitrogen, which softens growth and draws aphids.

records.our_prose: Collards is thin-sourced for the maritime PNW specifically (absent by name from both OSU's EM9027 and WSU's EM057E planting tables), so this cell is modeled on the crop's own established mild-zone pattern elsewhere, re-anchored to the region's real, milder frost dates. Direct sow or set transplants out a few weeks ahead of the last frost, then sow again in late summer for a fall and winter crop; as the hardiest cole crop, collards tolerates this region's light frosts well and keeps producing through nearly the entire year, pausing only around the two sowing windows themselves. The mild maritime winter should let the fall crop run later here than in a harder-frost climate, though that specific extension is not independently sourced for this region.

records.our_prose: The Gulf and coastal plain are collard country, where the crop grows nearly year-round. Plant in late winter for a spring-into-summer crop and again in late summer for a fall-and-winter crop; collards keep producing right through the hot, humid summer with even moisture, where lettuce and most brassicas cannot. Midsummer leaves are a touch tougher and pest pressure (harlequin bugs, caterpillars, aphids) peaks, so quality is best in the cool shoulders.

records.our_prose: Collards grow twice a year in St. George. Set plants out about February 15, USU Extension's St. George date, for tender leaves by late April. Collards shrug off more heat than most cole crops, but St. George's June heat is still too much, so let the bed rest and set a second round from mid-June to mid-July, following cabbage's fall window, for leaves into September. Frost returns around November 1.

records.our_prose: You can sow collard seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. Space full-size plants 18 to 24 inches apart. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.

records.our_prose: Collards can be direct sown or transplanted, and in the South direct sowing is the norm. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; collards tolerate frost. For a fall and winter crop, sow in mid to late summer so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in mild zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days. Thin or set plants 18 to 24 inches apart for full-size plants.
